intro: Cesky Krumlov's protected trees split in two directions. Four cluster eight kilometres out at Zlata Koruna, a Cistercian monastery: three behind its ticket, plus one free lime on the village square nearby, at 600 to 800 years the oldest tree here and older than the monastery itself. The other two stand roadside in opposite hamlets, a bridge oak and a hedge-lime nobody has dated. Nothing stands inside the old town's own walls; every tree here is a trip out from it, on foot, by train or by bike along the Vltava.
meta_description: Cesky Krumlov's oldest tree, 600 to 800 years, stands free on a village square by a monastery whose own lindens need a ticket.
question_answer: The oldest tree mapped here is the Cistercian Linden of Zlata Koruna, a large-leaved lime on the village square about 150 metres from Zlata Koruna monastery's gate, assessed at roughly 600 to 800 years old from measurements taken in the 1990s. It also happens to be the free one: the monastery's own trees nearby, including a taller, better-known lime in its courtyard, all sit behind the paid tour route.
question_meta: The Cistercian Linden on Zlata Koruna's village square, roughly 600 to 800 years old and free to see, just outside the monastery gate.
question_context: Zlata Koruna, a Cistercian monastery founded in 1263 by King Premysl Otakar II, about eight kilometres from Cesky Krumlov's old town, holds four of this page's six trees, three of them inside its paid grounds, now run as a state heritage site with its own admission and opening hours, closed Mondays. The exception is the oldest: a village-square lime whose lower trunk was packed with stone in the 19th century and whose upper trunk is still bound with metal bands, standing on open ground the monastery's ticket never touches. The Czech national register of memorial trees (pamatne stromy) gives species and girth for every tree here but no age field at all, so ages come from a mix of designation-era assessments, a documented abbot's tenure, and honest gaps where nothing survives. The other two trees, a bridge oak and a roadside lime, stand in separate hamlets in the opposite direction from Zlata Koruna and are best treated as their own short trips rather than part of one walk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cesky Krumlov?
faq.a: The Cistercian Linden of Zlata Koruna, roughly 600 to 800 years old, on the village square about 150 metres from the monastery gate. It is free to see.

faq.q: Can I see all six trees in one visit?
faq.a: Not in one walk. Four stand together at Zlata Koruna, eight kilometres from the old town; the other two are roadside trees in separate hamlets, Stare Dobrkovice and Drahoslavice, each its own short trip.
Half are. The village-square lime at Zlata Koruna and the two hamlet trees need no ticket. The other three, all inside Zlata Koruna monastery's grounds, are on the paid tour route.

faq.q: How do I get to Zlata Koruna?
faq.a: By train on the Ceske Budejovice to Cesky Krumlov to Cerny Kriz line, then a 15 to 20 minute walk downhill into the village, or about 8km by car or bike along the Vltava from Cesky Krumlov's old town.

trees.name: The Cistercian Linden of Zlatá Koruna

location.address: Village square (náves), in front of house no. 26, Zlatá Koruna
location.neighbourhood: Zlatá Koruna village, near Český Krumlov

verified_sources: AOPK CR national pamatny strom (memorial tree) register, entry supplied with coordinates in the city brief (register itself counts as one source per BRIEF_RESEARCH.md)
trees.access: Free, on the public village square in Zlata Koruna. Not part of the monastery's ticketed grounds, though it stands only about 150 metres from the gate.
trees.transport: Zlatá Koruna train station (line České Budějovice-Český Krumlov-Černý Kříž) then a roughly 15-20 minute walk downhill into the village; about 8km / 20-25 minutes by car or bike from Český Krumlov's old town, along the Vltava.
trees.story:
Part of this trunk is stonework. Some time in the 19th century masons packed and reinforced the hollowing base of the village lime with masonry, and the upper trunk is held together with metal bands so that it does not split under its own weight. What they were propping up is the oldest tree in Zlatá Koruna and, by the Blanský les landscape administration's reckoning, the oldest in the whole protected area: 7.18 metres round when the ministry's assessors measured it in 1994, 17 to 18 metres tall, and somewhere between 600 and 800 years old.

It did not always stand alone. A 17th-century chronicle describes it as one tree in an avenue of lindens running through the village, and this is the last of that line still standing. It was already several centuries old when the Cistercian abbey across the green was dissolved in 1785, and it has outlasted the monastery as a working institution by another two hundred and forty years.

The best part is the address. It stands on the public green in front of house number 26, about 150 metres outside the monastery gate, which means no ticket, no opening hours and no closed Monday. The state protects it twice over, as a memorial tree since 1990 and a national one since 1994. Walk up and stand under it.
trees.how_to_recognise: The big lime on Zlata Koruna's village square, in front of house no. 26, its lower trunk packed with stone and its upper trunk bound with metal bands.

trees.name: The Kapucínka Linden of Zlatá Koruna

location.address: Main courtyard of Zlatá Koruna monastery, beside the Chapel of the Guardian Angels, Zlatá Koruna
location.neighbourhood: Zlatá Koruna monastery (Klášter Zlatá Koruna), near Český Krumlov

trees.access: Inside Zlata Koruna monastery, a paid national heritage site (from about 180 Kc, discounts available, closed Mondays; roughly 09:00-15:30 April-May, 09:00-16:30 June-August).
trees.transport: Zlatá Koruna train station (line České Budějovice-Český Krumlov-Černý Kříž) then a roughly 15-20 minute walk downhill; about 8km / 20-25 minutes by car or bike from Český Krumlov's old town.
trees.story:
The leaves curl into hoods. That is a real mutation rather than a trick of the light: this lime grows in the cucullata form of Tilia platyphyllos, whose leaf blades roll up at the edges into small cowls, and the tree's Czech name, Kapucínka, comes from that shape.

The story attached to the name is older and darker than the tree itself. In 1420 Hussite troops took the monastery, and by local tradition the monks were hanged from the lindens of the avenue that then ran through the grounds. The hooded leaves have been read as a memorial of it ever since. The arithmetic does not support the reading. This tree is put at about 400 years old, which starts it roughly two centuries after the Hussites came through, so whatever it stands for it did not see.

What it did see is everything after: the abbey dissolved by imperial decree in 1785, the Schwarzenberg forestry school that briefly took over the buildings, and the long second life of the place as a state monument. It is the tallest of Zlatá Koruna's protected trees and the best known of them, 30 to 31 metres high and five metres round at the measurements taken in the mid 1990s, standing in the main courtyard beside the Chapel of the Guardian Angels. That courtyard is inside the ticket, and the monastery is closed on Mondays.
trees.how_to_recognise: The tall lime in the monastery's main courtyard beside the Chapel of the Guardian Angels; a second, smaller lime stands nearby in the same courtyard and is not this tree.

trees.name: The Cornelian Cherry of Zlatá Koruna

location.address: Garden of Zlatá Koruna monastery, Zlatá Koruna
location.neighbourhood: Zlatá Koruna monastery (Klášter Zlatá Koruna), near Český Krumlov

verified_sources: AOPK CR national pamatny strom (memorial tree) register, entry supplied with coordinates in the city brief
trees.access: Inside Zlata Koruna monastery's garden, on the guided tour route; same paid admission as the Kapucinka Linden.
trees.transport: Zlatá Koruna train station (line České Budějovice-Český Krumlov-Černý Kříž) then a roughly 15-20 minute walk downhill; about 8km / 20-25 minutes by car or bike from Český Krumlov's old town.

best_time.label: late August into September, when the scarlet drínky ripen along the branches

trees.story:
A cornelian cherry usually spends its life as a shrub. This one got to be a tree, and the monastery's own note on it says only that it still remembers the Cistercians, which is the Czech way of saying it was already growing here before the abbey was dissolved in 1785. No planting date has ever been written down, so the age stays loose on purpose: over two hundred years, and possibly a good deal more than that.

Its size is the figure to take carefully. The register puts the girth at 130 centimetres, unusually thick for Cornus mas and not confirmed by any second source. A species that tends to grow in clumps is easy to measure across several stems at once, and that may be what happened here.

What it does every year is not in doubt. In late summer the branches load with drínky, scarlet fruit the shape and size of a small olive, sour raw and very good cooked. Czech kitchens still turn them into jam and syrup, and before that the fruit was a folk remedy, which is a reasonable thing to find growing in a monastery garden. It flowers in the other direction too, bare yellow in the last weeks of winter, months before anything around it wakes up.

The tree stands in the garden on the tour route, so reaching it means the monastery ticket and its opening hours.
trees.how_to_recognise: A modest, shrub-like tree in the monastery garden section of the tour route, bearing small red fruit in late summer.

trees.name: The Silk Abbot's Mulberry

location.address: By the pond (vivárium), near the entrance gate of Zlatá Koruna monastery, Zlatá Koruna
location.neighbourhood: Zlatá Koruna monastery (Klášter Zlatá Koruna), near Český Krumlov

trees.access: Inside or right at the edge of Zlata Koruna monastery, by the pond near the entrance gate; treat as part of the paid tour route.
trees.transport: Zlatá Koruna train station (line České Budějovice-Český Krumlov-Černý Kříž) then a roughly 15-20 minute walk downhill; about 8km / 20-25 minutes by car or bike from Český Krumlov's old town.

best_time.label: July and August, when the fruit ripens almost black and drops

trees.story:
Zlatá Koruna's last abbot went into silk. Bohumír Bylanský ran the monastery until Joseph II dissolved it in 1785, and among the ventures he set up here was silkworm rearing, which meant planting mulberries to feed the worms. This tree is the last of those mulberries still standing, which puts it somewhere between 220 and 260 years old, counted back from the end of his tenure rather than from any recorded planting day.

Two details are worth holding lightly. Silkworms are normally raised on white mulberry; this is a black one, the species people plant when they are after the fruit. And the register's girth of 450 centimetres is very large for a mulberry trunk. Old black mulberries lean, spread and throw stems from low down, so that tape may have gone round more than one trunk, and no second measurement exists to check it against.

It still fruits. The monastery that planted it was shut down two and a half centuries ago and the silkworms are long gone, and every summer it drops black fruit onto the ground beside the monastery pond, which is where it grows, just inside the entrance gate. Getting to it means the monastery ticket and its opening hours, closed Mondays like the rest of the site.
trees.how_to_recognise: The mulberry by the pond near the monastery's entrance gate.

trees.name: The Bridge Oak of Staré Dobrkovice

location.address: By the historic stone bridge over the Polečnice river, left bank, Staré Dobrkovice, Český Krumlov
location.neighbourhood: Staré Dobrkovice, on the Kájov road out of Český Krumlov

verified_sources: AOPK CR national pamatny strom (memorial tree) register, code 106312, entry supplied with coordinates in the city brief
trees.access: Free, roadside, by the bridge over the Polecnice in Stare Dobrkovice; no gate or private land involved.
trees.transport: About 2.5km from Český Krumlov's old town along the Kájov road; roughly 30-35 minutes on foot, a few minutes by car or bike. No public transport stop confirmed right at the bridge.
trees.story:
The crash barrier runs in front of it. This oak stands at the mouth of an old stone bridge over the Polečnice in Staré Dobrkovice, on the left bank, close enough to the carriageway that the district's own record places it behind the road's safety barriers. A second oak stands at the far end of the bridge, so the two of them frame the crossing, though only this one is registered and documented as a protected tree.

It is a heavy tree: 4.15 metres round, a figure the national memorial-tree register and the Czech district list arrive at separately and agree on. The bridge beside it is a protected monument in its own right and was restored in 2021, which is why the stonework looks better cared for than the verge.

The setting is the point. This is the old road west out of Český Krumlov toward Kájov, about 2.5 kilometres from the painted houses of the old town, half an hour on foot down the river valley and a few minutes by bike. There is no gate, no ticket and no opening hour. You stand on the roadside, watch for traffic, and look up.

Nobody has dated it. The register kept its girth and not its years, and if you know how old this oak is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak on the left bank at the mouth of the stone bridge over the Polecnice in Stare Dobrkovice; a second oak stands on the far bank.

trees.access: Appears to stand free and in the open beside route 1572 at the edge of Drahoslavice, though nobody has confirmed this on the ground.
trees.transport: About 2.4km from Český Krumlov's old town along route 1572 toward Přídolí; roughly 30 minutes on foot, a few minutes by car or bike. No public transport stop confirmed at Drahoslavice itself.
trees.story:
The official record fixes this tree's position by the village weighbridge. It grows about ten metres from the váha at the eastern edge of Drahoslavice, a hamlet of a few houses on the road to Přídolí, which is a modest address for a tree of this size. The lime here runs to 32 metres tall and 5.13 metres round, one of the largest small-leaved limes anywhere near Český Krumlov, and the state has protected it since December 1990.

The lime is the Czech national tree, planted at crossroads, chapels and village greens all over Bohemia, and usually planted to mark something: a boundary, a coronation, a peace, a birth. Nobody wrote down what this one marks, if anything. It stands where the settlement ends and the fields start, and the road has been routed past it rather than through it.

By every description on record it stands in the open beside route 1572, with no fence, yard or gate between the tarmac and the trunk, though nobody has walked out to confirm that on the ground. Drahoslavice is about 2.4 kilometres from the old town, roughly half an hour uphill on foot and a few minutes by car or bike.

Its age is not known. No source gives one, so if you have a figure for this lime, or a tape measure, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: A large lime at the edge of Drahoslavice, about 10 metres from the local weighing station, beside route 1572.
